title: North Korea Says Smaller U.S. Drills Still Feel Threatening
summary: Have you ever had a neighbor who gets mad no matter what you do? That's kind of how North Korea feels about military drills between the U.S. and South Korea. The U.S. decided to make the drills smaller and shorter. They thought North Korea might like that. But North Korea said, "No thanks, it doesn't change anything." Kim Yo Jong is the sister of North Korea's leader, Kim Jong Un. She said the drills are still "provocative" and "aggressive" even if they are smaller. She also said there are no secret talks between her brother and President Trump. Earlier, Trump said Kim had responded to his request for a conversation. But Kim Yo Jong denied it. She did say her brother has "good memories" of Trump and their relationship is "great." That's a little nicer than usual. The drills are called Ulchi Freedom Shield. They usually last 11 days. Now they will end early, on Friday instead of August 27. Some field training is canceled or turned into computer simulations. The Pentagon says training goals are still met. But some experts worry that if drills stop for a long time, new commanders won't know the plans. The U.S. and South Korea have been allies since the Korean War in the 1950s. North Korea hates these drills. They think it's practice for an invasion. Just days before the drills started, North Korea launched two missiles into the sea. Some experts think Trump cut the drills to pressure South Korea to help with Iran, not to make peace with North Korea. South Korea's president hopes the friendly relationship between Trump and Kim will lead to real talks. But for now, North Korea isn't impressed.
why_it_matters: Countries sometimes use drills and strong words as signals, just like angry neighbors—understanding those signals helps you follow why wars or peace talks happen.

background_read: North Korea and South Korea are neighbors on the Korean Peninsula and have been separate countries since the Korean War in the 1950s.
Kim Jong Un (North Korea's leader) and his sister Kim Yo Jong often criticize U.S.-South Korean military drills.
President Donald Trump (the U.S. president since 2025) has said he has a friendly relationship with Kim Jong Un, but North Korea still sends tough messages.
